newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Mercedes pins growth on small A class car.
newsitem.headline: Mercedes pins growth on small A class car.

text.p: Mercedes-Benz AG, a giant among luxury carmakers but an admitted dwarf in the global industry, is counting on its new A class vehicle -- the smallest production car in Mercedes history -- for future growth.

The five-door hatchback, unveiled late on Monday at the Geneva car show, is key to Mercedes' aim of targeting younger buyers as part of a goal to reach annual sales of about one million vehicles by the turn of the century.

Mercedes plans to annually build about 200,000 of the new car, which was developed in 38 months for $1.65 billion, and will now face a fight from carmakers such as Volkswagen AG and General Motors Corp's Opel AG.

But Mercedes executives claim the German carmaker, which sold 645,000 cars in 1996, will not sell its luxury brand soul to become a high-volume carmaker and will still remain a niche player and premium car manufacturer.

Instead, Mercedes wants the A class to broaden its appeal to new target groups which were often out of reach. The A class will have base price of about 30,000 marks ($17,500), less than half the cost for many of Mercedes' more upscale luxury saloons.

"Far from posing a risk for the Mercedes-Benz brand, the A class is actually very necessary and important in helping us achieve the kind of public perception that we want," said Dieter Zetsche, Mercedes's top sales and marketing executive.
The new A class comes at a critical time for Mercedes, which has sought to attract younger affluent car buyers as well as enter emerging markets to expand its customer base.
The existing line of Mercedes products competes in a luxury market segment of only about three million annual vehicle sales out of a total worldwide market of around 39 million cars.

"Although we had a share of over 20 percent in this competitive segment, in volume terms we are nevertheless a dwarf," said Juergen Hubbert, the Mercedes management board member in charge of passenger car sales.

Hubbert said the addition of the A class, along with joint ventures in emerging markets such as India and Asia, will help triple the potential market for Mercedes cars to about nine million annual vehicle sales by the year 2000.

Mercedes executives had their work cut out for them in designing the A class, which the carmaker says is a blend of the subcompact class, the compact class, the lower mid-range class and the compact van.

Mercedes argues it has created a new class of vehicles with the A class, considered one of the smallest cars in Europe, saying it should not be a "copycat" product or some sort of a derivative of the long-popular Volkswagen Golf.
The result is a snappy car with a four-cylinder engine that comes equipped with driver and passenger airbags, anti-lock brakes, traction control and door-mounted airbags as standard.
Designers started from scratch with a goal to create a car for 30-something singles, two-person households and young families at a time of difficult sales for luxury carmakers.

The target group was a far cry from the traditional older Mercedes buyer and required the German carmaker to revamp many of its dealerships and to train sales staff to handle a younger target audience ahead of the car's rollout to European dealers in May. Mercedes has no current plans to sell it in the U.S.
The carmaker also created an Internet web site to attract potential customers along with a direct-mail campaign that has so far received about 300,000 positive responses.
Mercedes will build the car at its Rastatt factory in Germany in only 16 hours. That compares with 26 hours for the C class, the next step up in the Mercedes product line.

Juergen Schrempp, who took over in January as chief of Mercedes after he folded the carmaker into parent Daimler-Benz AG, said it was a "burning question" for executives whether they could maintain Mercedes quality in a subcompact.
"Now the question has been answered," Schrempp said at the unveiling of the car, which is only 3.60 meters long and 1.60 meters tall. "The A class deserves its Mercedes star."
($ = 1.707 German Marks)
